finding.title: Agent MEMORY.md auto-injection is unbudgeted: up to 20.8KB (~6.3k tokens) injected per dispatch, 502-file/1.73MB corpus growing with no size rule [CONFIRMED]
finding.mechanism: All 18 agents have `memory: project`; the harness injects .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md into every dispatch of that agent. The kit budgets SPRINT_STATE (≤6KB BINDING) and wiki pages (<50KB) but sets NO budget for MEMORY.md indexes, which grow monotonically with every sprint (consolidate-memory runs only kratno-5 at session level and does not enforce per-agent index size).
finding.evidence: `grep -l 'memory: project' ~/.claude/agents/*.md` → 18/18. MEMORY.md sizes: doc-writer 20,841 B (146 lines), architecture-reviewer 19,596 B, trading-logic-reviewer 18,207 B, quant-stats-reviewer 17,556 B, doc-reviewer-depth 14,222 B, security-auditor 12,286 B; 120,474 B total across 14 indexes; whole corpus 502 .md files / 1,733,929 B. A standard 6-reviewer parallel round injects ~100KB ≈ ~30k tokens of memory alone, on top of agent system prompts (204,200 B total for 18 agents, max trading-logic-reviewer 23,319 B); the observed 21-writer batch (2026-06-26) ≈ 21 × 20.8KB ≈ 130k tokens of doc-writer memory injection in one phase. `grep MEMORY.md` across all 3 CLAUDE.md filtered for KB/budget/бюджет/строк → 0 hits: no budget rule exists anywhere.
finding.why_weak: Injection cost scales linearly with sprint count and is already the largest per-dispatch overhead for the busiest agents (doc-writer memory ≈ 2× its own system prompt; architecture-reviewer memory > prompt). Sampled content (doc-writer) is a healthy link-index — the defect is the absence of a ceiling, not quality: without one, token loss compounds silently every future sprint.
finding.proposed_direction: Add a BINDING budget mirroring SPRINT_STATE: MEMORY.md ≤ 8KB (index lines + topic-file links only; details stay in topic files — already the observed pattern). Enforce mechanically: kit-inventory/hooks-selfcheck WARN at >8KB (on the D7-01-fixed visible channel) and add per-agent 'merge/prune index when over budget' to the consolidate-memory cadence.

verdicts.reasoning: Core finding CONFIRMED — evidence reproduces almost byte-exact and none of the refutation criteria fire. (1) Reproduction: 18/18 agents in ~/.claude/agents/ carry `memory: project`; MEMORY.md sizes match the finding exactly (doc-writer 20,841 B / 146 lines, architecture-reviewer 19,596 B, trading-logic-reviewer 18,207 B, quant-stats-reviewer 17,556 B, doc-reviewer-depth 14,222 B); agent prompt corpus totals 204,200 B with trading-logic-reviewer 23,319 B — both exact. Growth is directly observed, not speculative: security-auditor grew 12,286→12,702 B, corpus grew 502→504 files / 1,733,929→1,739,892 B, MEMORY.md sum 120,474→121,080 B since the finding was written days ago. (2) Not fixed in S57-S67: sprint pages 57-67 and ADRs 0070-0076 contain zero MEMORY.md-size work; S62 «budget-ревизия» did not touch agent memory. (3) Not already tracked: UNIFIED-BACKLOG-S57 KIT-021 is about MISSING memory dirs (different defect); kit-op-detect-hardening-backlog and error-taxonomy.md have zero agent-memory hits; no mechanical check in kit/hooks/*.sh or kit-inventory. (4) No operator decision contradicted. Two accuracy corrections that do NOT refute: (a) the claim «no budget rule exists anywhere» is overstated — 11/18 agent prompts DO contain self-maintenance budgets (≤200 lines / 25KB; doc-reviewer 12KB, kit-auditor/merge-analyst 18KB, e.g. kit/agents/security-auditor.md:38). But these are discipline-only (agent self-edits, no mechanical WARN), 7/18 agents have NO budget line at all — including doc-writer, the largest index, plus doc-reviewer-depth, doc-linker, trader-expert — and the line-based variants don't bound bytes (trading-logic = 18.2KB in only 36 lines). Existing 25KB ceilings are 3× the proposed 8KB and above SPRINT_STATE's 6KB, so the unbounded-overhead mechanism stands. (b) «6-reviewer round ≈ 100KB ≈ 30k tokens» is inflated: the standard L5 six (trading-logic+quant-stats+data-integrity+architecture+python+security) sums to 71,146 B ≈ ~21.5k tokens at 3.3 B/token. Order of magnitude holds; the doc-writer 21× batch math (20.8KB each) is arithmetically sound. Proposed direction should harmonize with the EXISTING prompt-level budgets (extend to all 18, add byte cap, mechanize the check) rather than introduce a rule «from scratch».

What remains true is a much narrower residue than stated: the 25KB cap is prompt discipline (not mechanically enforced), 9 lower-traffic agents lack an explicit numeric cap, and a 200-line cap does not bound bytes (architecture-reviewer packs 20KB into 47 lines). That residue is a LOW-grade hygiene item ("mechanize + unify the existing cap"), not the claimed "unbudgeted, no size rule" MEDIUM.

finding.title: 14 sequential PreToolUse hooks × ~16 python3 spawns per Bash call — ~0.46s benign / ~0.92s push overhead with no shared prefilter
finding.mechanism: settings.json wires 14 hooks under one PreToolUse Bash matcher, run sequentially. On EVERY Bash tool call each hook independently `cat`s the payload and spawns python3 to extract `tool_input.command`, then most early-exit because the command isn't push/commit/merge/read. 16 of the 17 .sh files contain a python3 spawn. There is no cheap shared prefilter, so a plain `git status` still pays ~14 interpreter startups.
finding.evidence: Measured (env, 3 runs, stable): benign `git status` payload through the 14-hook chain = real 0.46s ×3; `git push origin main` payload = real 0.92/0.91/0.97s. Single `python3 -c pass` = 0.02s. `grep -l python3 ~/.claude/hooks/*.sh | wc -l` = 16. Over a mega-run issuing thousands of Bash tool calls this is minutes-to-hours of cumulative wall-clock latency (no token cost).
finding.why_weak: The kit's stated goal is 'work like a fine watch — max token/time economy', but the gate layer imposes a fixed ~0.5s tax on every Bash call, 90%+ of which match no gate. The per-hook duplicate JSON-parse is pure redundancy.
finding.proposed_direction: Either (a) a single dispatcher hook parses the command once and routes to the relevant gate (push→push-gates, commit→state/pertask, merge→review/phase), or (b) give each hook a cheap `case "$payload" in *push*|*commit*|*merge*) ;; *) exit 0 ;; esac` raw-string prefilter BEFORE the python3 spawn. Preserves behavior, cuts ~14 spawns to ~1 on the dominant benign path. Cross-domain: architecture-reviewer for the dispatcher design.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding's headline mechanism — "14 sequential PreToolUse hooks... ~0.46s benign / ~0.92s push overhead" — does not survive independent checking because Claude Code does NOT run hooks sequentially. Official docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) state verbatim: "All matching hooks run in parallel, and identical handlers are deduplicated automatically." The finding's measurement replayed the 14 hooks in a sequential bash loop (I reproduced its exact numbers that way: 0.46-0.48s benign, 0.90-0.92s push), but re-measuring under the documented parallel model gives ~0.06s benign and ~0.15s push per Bash call — 8× and 6× lower than claimed. A ~60ms parallel-wall-clock tax per Bash call is noise relative to the multi-second model round-trip each tool call already costs, so the projected impact ("minutes-to-hours of cumulative wall-clock latency over a mega-run") is derived from a wrong execution model and is speculative — no observed instance of hook latency bottlenecking a run exists. Additionally, per-hook cost was already explicitly assessed and accepted as negligible in ADR 0046 (llm-wiki/wiki/project/decisions/0046-sprint-32b-kit-phase-1-improvements.md:94: "Per-hook cost ~50-100ms (negligible)") — the real parallel figure today (60-150ms) is still inside that accepted band despite the chain growing 7→14. What survives is only a LOW-grade hygiene observation: each hook does redundantly cat+python3-parse the same payload before its case prefilter (16/17 .sh files spawn python3; state-integrity/state-backup/pertask/sprint-flow etc. all parse before filtering; cascade-read-check pipes the payload to python3 unconditionally), so ~14 CPU spawns per Bash call do happen — but in parallel, costing ~1 spawn of wall-clock. A raw-string prefilter or dispatcher would be a micro-optimization with no measurable effect on run duration; it is not a MEDIUM weakness, and the proposed single-dispatcher redesign would add a new single point of failure (one broken dispatcher = ALL gates fail-OPEN, worsening the P1-BASHN class) for no measurable gain.

The finding's 0.46s/0.92s measurements (and my reproduction: 0.51-0.54s benign, 1.03-1.07s push) come from a hand-rolled loop that pipes the payload through the 14 hooks one at a time — a sequentialism imposed by the measurement harness, not by Claude Code.
